metadata.title: Risk Management Plans to Mitigate the Potential for Drug Shortages
metadata.topic: Draft guideline · FDA human drugs and biologics

candidates.statement: 11 Generally, section 506C(a) of the FD&C Act, as amended by FDASIA (Public Law 112-144) and the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (Public Law 116-136), requires certain applicants and manufacturers to notify the Agency of: (1) a permanent discontinuance in the manufacture of certain drug products; (2) an interruption in manufacturing of certain drug products that is likely to lead to a meaningful disruption in the supply of such products in the United States; (3) a permanent discontinuance in the manufacture of the API of certain drug products; and (4) an interruption in the manufacture of the API of certain drug products that is likely to lead to a meaningful disruption in the supply of the API of those products. Notifications under section 506C(a) must include disclosure of the reasons for such discontinuance or interruption. Section 506E of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 356e) requires FDA to maintain an up-to-date list of drugs that are determined by FDA to be in shortage in the United States. Section 711 of FDASIA amended section 501 of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 351) to clarify that, for purposes of section 501(a)(2)(B), the term current good manufacturing practice includes the implementation of oversight and controls over the manufacture of drugs to ensure quality, including managing the risk of and establishing the safety of raw materials, materials used in the manufacturing of drugs, and finished drug products.

candidates.statement: RMPs help to ensure that risks with the potential to disrupt the drug manufacturing process and 246 the drug supply chain have been identified, assessed, and mitigated. An individual stakeholder’s 247 role in developing and implementing an RMP varies with that stakeholder’s level of involvement 248 with the drug manufacturing process or supply chain. Nonetheless, FDA believes that risk 249 management principles should be applied throughout the drug supply chain to help mitigate the 250 risk of drug shortages. 251
candidates.context: A. candidates.statement: The Agency recommends at least an annual, internal review and revision of an RMP throughout 349 the life cycle of a drug. RMP review and revision should include lessons learned, including the 350 root cause of new and near-miss supply disruptions. In some instances, it may be useful to 351 quickly integrate the additional identified risks and mitigation strategies into the RMP rather than 352 waiting for the next annual review cycle. This review also can include an assessment of 353 communication with regulators and whether the communication should be improved. 354

candidates.statement: Certain stakeholders are required to submit notifications to the Agency about drug product and 362 API permanent discontinuances and certain manufacturing interruptions under section 506C of 363 the FD&C Act. 53 , 54 For the notifications received, FDA works with the stakeholder to assess the 364 situation and prevent or mitigate any shortage that may result, when possible. Stakeholders that 365 are covered by the notification requirement under section 506C must submit certain information 366 to FDA as part of the notification. 55 Along with the information that is required to be submitted, 367 the Agency recommends that manufacturers provide additional information that may assist the 368 Agency in addressing the situation. FDA has published a list of questions for manufacturers to 369 consider as they evaluate the situation and prepare to notify FDA, including whether the 370 manufacturer has a proposal for FDA to review to expedite availability of a product. 56 This 371 information would likely be contained in an RMP. candidates.statement: RMPs for Secondary Stakeholders and Other Stakeholders — When a stakeholder that is not 484 the primary stakeholder (i.e., a secondary or other stakeholder) develops its RMP, it typically 485 should interpret the broader risks identified in the primary stakeholder’s RMP within the context 486 of a specific manufacturing facility, and address unique risks at a manufacturing facility that are 487 unlikely to be identified by the primary stakeholder. Furthermore, many of the risks might have 488 specific implications to the drugs manufactured at a facility (e.g., environmental controls might 489 affect a sterile, parenteral drug more than a solid, oral dosage drug). The RMP for stakeholders 490 that are not the primary stakeholder should consider the effect of identified risks on the 491 manufacturing facility as well as on the drugs manufactured at that facility. The following non- 492 exhaustive list provides risk factors for such stakeholders to consider as part of developing an 493 RMP. Some of these risk factors may also be useful to the primary stakeholder, depending on 494 the responsibilities of the primary stakeholder. 495
